items.stem: Why should an interrupt service routine (ISR) be kept short and avoid blocking?

options.text: A long ISR delays other interrupts and can cause missed events or latency
options.rationale: Correct: ISRs should do minimal work and defer the rest.

options.text: ISRs run only once per power cycle
options.rationale: They run on each triggering event.

options.text: A long ISR speeds up the main loop

items.explanation: Correct: ISRs should do minimal work and defer the rest.

items.stem: Why must a variable shared between an ISR and main code often be declared volatile?

options.text: It prevents the compiler from caching the value, ensuring each access reads the real memory
options.rationale: Correct: volatile stops optimisations that would miss ISR updates.

options.text: It makes the variable thread-safe by itself
It allocates the variable on the heap
It speeds up access to the variable
options.rationale: It typically prevents caching, not speeds up.

items.explanation: Correct: volatile stops optimisations that would miss ISR updates.

items.stem: Which statements about embedded development are correct? (Select TWO)

options.text: Hardware timers/PWM are preferred over busy-wait delays for periodic tasks
options.rationale: Correct: timers free the CPU and keep timing accurate.

options.text: A peripheral often needs its clock enabled before use
options.rationale: Correct: forgetting the clock gate is a common bug.

options.text: Embedded targets typically have abundant RAM like desktops
Dynamic allocation in a tight loop is best practice on MCUs
options.rationale: False; it risks fragmentation and is usually avoided.

items.explanation: Correct: timers free the CPU and keep timing accurate.; Correct: forgetting the clock gate is a common bug.
